definition: A step-by-step method for completing a task safely and consistently.
example: Students followed the SOP for grinder setup, use, and shutdown before starting work.

definition: Recognizing anything that could cause harm in the shop (equipment, process, material, environment, or behaviour).
example: Students identified pinch points at a vise, hot surfaces, and trip hazards in walkways.

definition: Estimating how likely harm is to occur and how severe the harm could be.
example: Grinding without a face shield was assessed as high risk due to likely eye/face injury.

definition: A safety strategy that prioritizes eliminating hazards, then engineering controls, administrative controls, and PPE last.
example: Students used guards and ventilation (engineering controls) rather than relying only on PPE.

definition: Protective gear worn to reduce exposure to hazards.
example: Students wore safety glasses, hearing protection, and gloves when cutting and grinding.

definition: Moving/removing air to reduce exposure to fumes, dust, and vapours.
example: Students positioned fume extraction near grinding to reduce airborne particulate.

definition: Maintaining a clean, organized, hazard-free work area.
example: After cutting, students cleared offcuts, swept dust, and returned tools to storage.

definition: Checking tools for damage, correct setup, and safe operation before use.
example: Students confirmed the grinder guard was secure and the disc was rated for the tool speed.

definition: Securing material so it can be worked on safely and accurately.
example: Tubing was clamped square to the table before marking and cutting.

definition: A device that holds material together or to a surface during layout, cutting, or assembly.
example: Two clamps prevented tubing from shifting during a mitre cut.

definition: A tool used to set or verify 90-degree angles during layout and assembly.
example: Students checked corners with a square before final assembly.

definition: Removing sharp edges and burrs after cutting or drilling to improve safety and fit.
example: Students deburred holes so bolts seated correctly and parts were safe to handle.

definition: Items used up during fabrication work (discs, blades, marking tools, wire, gas).
example: Cut-off wheels and flap discs were tracked as consumables for the project.

definition: Planned upkeep that reduces breakdowns and keeps tools operating safely.
example: Students cleaned tools, checked cords, and stored equipment properly to prevent damage.

definition: Metal that contains iron (often magnetic), such as steel.
example: Students identified mild steel as ferrous using a magnet test.

definition: Metal with little or no iron, such as aluminum or copper.
example: Students separated non-ferrous scrap into the correct bin for sorting and recycling.

definition: A mixture of metals (or metal with other elements) designed to improve properties.
example: Students discussed why stainless steel (an alloy) resists corrosion better than mild steel.

definition: Characteristics that affect performance (strength, hardness, ductility, toughness, corrosion resistance).
example: Mild steel was selected for beginner fabrication because it is more ductile and forgiving.

definition: Oil, paint, rust, or debris on material that reduces accuracy and quality.
example: Students cleaned rust and oil before layout so marks were accurate and visible.

definition: Determining size or distance using tools and a reference point.
example: Students measured stock, verified twice, then marked cut lines using a reference edge.

definition: Marking material to guide cutting, drilling, bending, or assembly.
example: Students laid out hole locations and centre-punched before drilling.

definition: A chosen edge used as the starting point for measurements to reduce accumulated error.
example: All hole offsets were measured from one reference edge so parts matched reliably.

definition: The allowable variation from a target dimension.
example: Tubing was cut within tolerance so the frame assembled square without forcing parts.

definition: How close a measurement is to the true value.
example: Students improved accuracy by using a square and marking with a scribe rather than a marker.

definition: How consistent repeated measurements are.
example: Students produced multiple matching parts by repeating the same layout process precisely.

definition: A list of parts to cut, including dimensions, quantities, and material type.
example: Students created a cut list for all tubing pieces before starting any cuts.

definition: A list of required materials and quantities needed to complete a project.
example: The BOM included plate thickness, tubing sizes, consumables, and fasteners.

definition: A planned sequence of tasks, tools, safety steps, and checks for a build.
example: Students planned: measure, cut, deburr, fit-up, check square, assemble, inspect, finish.

definition: An organized method for managing people, tools, materials, and steps to produce consistent results.
example: The class used stations (layout, cutting, finishing) so multiple groups could work efficiently.

definition: Making multiple identical parts in groups to improve efficiency and consistency.
example: Students cut and deburred all identical pieces as a batch before assembly.

definition: A step that limits workflow because it has the least capacity or takes the most time.
example: Deburring became the bottleneck until the class added a second finishing station.

definition: Checking work against requirements to confirm it meets standards and to find defects.
example: QC checks included length, squareness, and safe edges before assembly.

definition: Preventing defects by building checks and standards into the process from the start.
example: QA included measuring after each cut so errors were caught early, not at final assembly.

definition: Hollow material supplied as tube used for frames and structures.
example: Students used square tubing to build a frame and checked corners for squareness.

definition: Solid metal supplied as bars (round, square, flat) used for brackets and parts.
example: Students cut flat bar stock into brackets according to the cut list.

definition: The thickness of the tube wall, affecting strength, weight, and cutting approach.
example: Students selected wall thickness that balanced strength with ease of cutting and fit-up.

definition: An angled cut used so tubing joins cleanly at corners or intersections.
example: Students cut 45-degree mitres so frame corners met tightly with minimal gaps.

definition: The width of material removed by a cutting process.
example: Students accounted for kerf so final lengths matched the cut list.

definition: How parts are positioned and held so they match the intended layout before joining or final assembly.
example: Students improved fit-up by deburring, clamping, and checking corners with a square.

definition: How close an angle is to 90 degrees, often checked on frames and assemblies.
example: Students measured diagonals to confirm the rectangular frame was square.

definition: A guide that helps position a tool or part to repeat an operation accurately.
example: A drilling jig ensured every bracket had matching hole spacing.

definition: A device or setup that holds parts in a repeatable position for consistent work.
example: A corner fixture helped groups assemble multiple frames more efficiently.

definition: A technical drawing that communicates design intent, dimensions, and specifications.
example: Students used the drawing to create a BOM and verify dimensions before cutting.

definition: A drawing view that shows an object from one direction (front, top, side).
example: Students used the top view to confirm spacing not obvious in the front view.

definition: A drawing that shows a 3D-like view to help visualize shape and assembly.
example: Students used the isometric view to understand how the bracket aligned on the frame.

definition: Tracking, storing, and returning tools so they are available and safe for the next user.
example: Students signed out specialty tools and returned them clean, inspected, and stored correctly.

definition: Meeting workplace expectations: safety, punctuality, respect, and accountability.
example: Students reported a hazard, paused work, and documented the issue before continuing.

definition: The information panel on a drawing that identifies the part, drawing number, revision, scale, units, and other key details.
example: Before measuring anything, students checked the title block for scale and units to avoid building the wrong size.

definition: The ratio between drawing size and real size (full-size, reduced, or enlarged).
example: A detail was shown at a larger scale so small features could be read clearly.

definition: The measurement system used on a drawing (metric or imperial).
example: Students confirmed the drawing was in millimetres before cutting stock.

definition: Written instructions on a drawing that apply to the whole part or project (materials, tolerances, finishes, processes).
example: General notes specified deburring all edges, so students planned finishing time into the job.

definition: A tracked version of a drawing that records updates and changes from earlier versions.
example: Students verified the current revision letter matched the latest print before starting fabrication.

definition: Standard drawing lines that communicate different information (visible, hidden, centre, dimension, section).
example: Hidden lines showed internal features that were not visible from the outside view.

definition: A line that marks the centre of a circle, hole, cylinder, or symmetrical feature.
example: The hole pattern was located using centrelines to ensure symmetry.

definition: The system of numbers, lines, and symbols that defines sizes and locations on a drawing.
example: Students used dimensioning to create a cut list and locate hole positions accurately.

definition: Dimensions taken from a single starting reference so errors do not stack across multiple measurements.
example: Hole locations were dimensioned from one baseline to prevent cumulative layout error.

definition: A series of dimensions placed end-to-end where each dimension begins where the last one ends.
example: Students noted chain dimensioning can stack small errors, so they measured carefully and rechecked.

definition: A drawing view showing a cut-through of an object to reveal interior details clearly.
example: A section view showed the internal step that needed to be machined, which was hidden in other views.

definition: A magnified view of a small area to show features and dimensions more clearly.
example: Students used a detail view to read the exact radius and edge-break callout.

definition: A view projected to show the true shape/size of features on an angled surface.
example: An auxiliary view clarified the true length of a bevel on an angled face.

definition: A note or specification on a drawing that states what material to use.
example: The material callout required mild steel, so students avoided mixing in unknown scrap.

definition: A note or symbol specifying surface finish or edge treatment requirements.
example: The print required deburring and a smooth finish on all hand-contact edges.

definition: A standardized note that defines a hole’s size and any special features (countersink, counterbore, depth).
example: A hole callout specified diameter and depth, so the drilling operation included a depth stop.

definition: A note identifying fastener type, size, thread, and length needed for assembly.
example: Students selected the correct bolt by reading the fastener callout rather than guessing.

definition: A system for labelling parts and assemblies so they match the print and do not get mixed up.
example: Students labelled each cut part with a part ID that matched the cut list and drawing.

definition: A force applied to a structure or component.
example: Students estimated the load on a bracket based on what it needed to hold in use.

definition: A constant load from the weight of the structure and permanently attached components.
example: The dead load included the weight of the frame itself and mounted hardware.

definition: A changing load from people, moving items, or temporary forces.
example: The live load increased when a person leaned on the railing or equipment shifted.

definition: A force concentrated at one location.
example: A single hanging hook created a point load on the crossmember.

definition: A force spread over a length or area.
example: Tools placed along a shelf created a distributed load across the supports.

definition: Internal force per unit area within a material caused by an external load.
example: Students discussed how smaller cross-sections create higher stress under the same load.

definition: How much a material deforms compared to its original length when loaded.
example: Students compared strain by observing deflection differences between two member sizes.

definition: Deformation that returns to original shape after the load is removed.
example: A beam that springs back after unloading experienced elastic deformation.

definition: Permanent deformation that remains after the load is removed.
example: A bent bracket that does not return to shape shows plastic deformation.

definition: The amount a structural member bends or moves under load.
example: Students measured deflection at mid-span to compare two beam designs.

definition: The way a part or structure stops working (bending, buckling, fracture, shear, fastener failure).
example: Students identified buckling as a likely failure mode for a long, slender compression member.

definition: Sudden sideways bending of a compression member when it becomes unstable.
example: A tall, thin member buckled under compression even though the material itself did not crush.

definition: The cross-section area where sliding failure can occur under shear forces (often in fasteners).
example: Students checked whether a bolt was loaded in single-shear or double-shear at the joint.

definition: A connection between members where forces are transferred (welded, bolted, riveted).
example: Students compared joint options based on load direction and future serviceability needs.

definition: A reinforcing plate used to strengthen a joint or connection area.
example: A gusset plate was added to reduce flex at a corner where two tubes met.

definition: The distance between a force and the point it rotates around; a longer arm increases bending effect.
example: Moving the load farther from the support increased the moment arm and the bending demand.

definition: A limitation that affects design choices (material, weight, size, cost, tools, time, safety).
example: A size constraint meant the bracket needed a different shape to maintain strength.

definition: The route forces take through a structure from where they are applied to where they are supported.
example: Students traced the load path to see which members carried the highest demand.

definition: A process that uses oxygen and a fuel gas to produce a flame for heating, brazing, soldering, or cutting.
example: Students used oxyfuel to preheat steel before bending and to perform oxyfuel cutting on plate.

definition: A combustible gas used with oxygen to create a high-temperature flame (commonly acetylene, but other fuels exist).
example: Students confirmed the correct fuel gas for the torch setup before lighting.

definition: A high-pressure cylinder that supplies oxygen for oxyfuel operations.
example: Students secured the oxygen cylinder upright and checked that the valve area was clean before use.

definition: A cylinder designed to safely store acetylene dissolved in a porous filler; handled differently from oxygen cylinders.
example: Students kept the acetylene cylinder upright and ensured it was properly secured on the cart.

definition: Using chains/straps and a proper cart to prevent cylinders from tipping or being damaged.
example: Students used two-point securing to prevent cylinders from shifting during movement.

definition: The main on/off control at the top of a cylinder that releases gas to the regulator.
example: Students opened the oxygen valve slowly to protect the regulator and gauges.

definition: A device that reduces cylinder pressure to a controllable working pressure.
example: Students adjusted the regulator to the correct working pressure for the selected tip size.

definition: The regulator gauge that shows the cylinder (supply) pressure.
example: Students checked the high-pressure gauge to confirm the cylinder had enough gas for the task.

definition: The regulator gauge that shows the pressure being delivered to the hose and torch.
example: Students verified working pressure before lighting to keep the flame stable.

definition: Flexible hoses that carry oxygen and fuel gas from regulators to the torch (typically colour-coded).
example: Students inspected hoses for cracks and ensured connections were tight before use.

definition: A safety device that prevents a flame from travelling back through the torch and hoses.
example: Students confirmed flashback arrestors were installed before operating the torch.

definition: A one-way valve that prevents reverse gas flow, reducing the risk of mixing gases in hoses.
example: Students verified check valves were oriented correctly during setup.

definition: Checking connections and equipment for leaks (commonly with approved leak-detection solution) before lighting.
example: Students applied leak solution to fittings and watched for bubbles before use.

definition: Briefly flowing gas through hoses/torch to remove mixed gases and ensure correct gas is present before lighting.
example: Students purged oxygen and fuel lines separately before igniting the torch.

definition: The main hand-held body of the torch with valves that control oxygen and fuel flow.
example: Students adjusted torch valves to achieve a steady flame during heating.

definition: A torch component that adds an oxygen cutting lever and is used with cutting tips for severing steel.
example: Students installed the cutting attachment when switching from welding/brazing to cutting.

definition: A designation that matches a torch tip to the material thickness and required heat input/flow.
example: Students selected a larger tip size for thicker plate to maintain proper preheat.

definition: A flint ignition tool used to light an oxyfuel torch safely.
example: Students used a striker rather than a lighter to ignite the fuel gas.

definition: A balanced oxyfuel flame (correct oxygen-to-fuel ratio) commonly used for general heating and welding applications.
example: Students tuned to a neutral flame before practicing controlled heating on scrap.

definition: A fuel-rich flame that can add carbon to steel surfaces and is used for specific heating/brazing conditions.
example: Students identified a carburizing flame by its feather and adjusted to the required setting for the task.

definition: An oxygen-rich flame that can oxidize metal surfaces and is used only for specific applications.
example: Students corrected an oxidizing flame when surface oxidation appeared during heating.

definition: Heating steel to ignition temperature prior to applying the cutting oxygen stream.
example: Students preheated the cut line until it reached the correct colour/temperature before pressing the lever.

definition: A control that releases a high-pressure oxygen stream to oxidize and blow molten metal out of the kerf.
example: After preheat, students pressed the lever to start the cut and maintain a steady travel speed.

definition: The high-velocity stream of oxygen that performs the cutting action by rapid oxidation and material removal.
example: Students maintained torch height so the oxygen jet stayed centred in the kerf.

definition: The width of material removed by the cut, affected by tip size, oxygen flow, and travel speed.
example: Students adjusted speed to reduce kerf width variation and improve edge quality.

definition: Vertical lines on a cut edge that indicate cutting speed and technique; their angle can show if travel speed is off.
example: Students reduced travel speed when drag lines became too angled and rough.

definition: Starting a cut by creating an initial hole through the material before moving along the cut line.
example: Students used a controlled pierce at the edge to avoid excessive spatter and blowback.

definition: Starting a cut from the edge of the material rather than piercing in the middle.
example: Students chose an edge start to reduce cleanup and improve safety on thicker plate.

definition: The orientation of the torch relative to the workpiece, affecting cut quality and dross formation.
example: Students kept the torch near-perpendicular for straight cuts and consistent kerf.

definition: The distance between the tip and the workpiece; critical for stable flame and clean cutting.
example: Students maintained consistent standoff to prevent popping and uneven cut edges.

definition: How fast the torch moves along the cut line, affecting kerf, drag lines, and dross.
example: Students slowed slightly on corners to keep the cut from lagging behind the preheat zone.

definition: Re-solidified molten material that sticks to the bottom edge of a cut, often caused by speed/pressure/heat issues.
example: Students reduced heavy dross by adjusting oxygen flow and travel speed.

definition: Solidified by-product from oxidation during cutting that may adhere to the cut edge.
example: Students chipped and brushed slag from the cut edge before fitting parts.

definition: The area beside a cut where heat changes material properties without melting.
example: Students planned extra grinding allowance where the HAZ needed cleanup before welding.

definition: Cutting an angled edge to prepare a joint or meet a design requirement.
example: Students bevel-cut plate edges to prepare for a stronger welded joint.

definition: Using an oxyfuel flame to heat metal for bending, straightening, loosening, or preheating.
example: Students applied controlled heat to straighten a slightly warped bar after fabrication.

definition: Joining metals by melting a filler metal that flows into the joint without melting the base metal.
example: Students brazed a joint using correct heat control so the filler flowed by capillary action.

definition: Low-temperature joining using a filler metal with a melting point below brazing, without melting base metal.
example: Students used soldering for a thin component where high heat would cause distortion.

definition: The added metal that melts and bonds parts in brazing or soldering.
example: Students selected the appropriate filler metal for the material combination being joined.

definition: A chemical used in brazing/soldering to clean surfaces and prevent oxidation so filler can bond properly.
example: Students applied flux to the joint area so the filler flowed smoothly and bonded cleanly.

definition: The movement of molten filler into a tight joint gap during brazing/soldering.
example: With correct joint gap and heat, the filler drew into the seam by capillary action.

definition: The small, controlled gap between parts that allows molten filler to flow and bond effectively.
example: Students adjusted fit so the clearance was consistent, improving filler flow and strength.

definition: A momentary pop where the flame goes out at the tip, often due to tip contact, incorrect pressures, or overheating.
example: When a backfire occurred, students shut down safely, checked the tip, and corrected settings.

definition: A dangerous condition where flame travels back into the torch and hoses, often accompanied by a squeal/hiss.
example: Students responded to a flashback by closing valves in the correct order and checking equipment before reuse.

definition: The correct order of closing valves and relieving pressures to safely end oxyfuel operation and store equipment.
example: Students closed torch valves, shut cylinder valves, bled lines, and backed off regulator screws before storage.

definition: A group of welding processes that use an electric arc to melt and join metals.
example: Students set polarity and parameters before striking an arc on mild steel coupons.

definition: The intense electrical discharge between electrode and workpiece that produces heat for welding.
example: A steady arc sound and consistent arc length helped maintain bead shape.

definition: The complete path electricity follows from the power source through the electrode, arc, workpiece, and back through the work lead.
example: Students checked for clean work lead contact to avoid an unstable arc.

definition: The cable and clamp that connects the workpiece to the welding power source (often called the ground clamp).
example: Students moved the work lead closer to the joint to reduce resistance and improve arc stability.

definition: The direction of current flow (electrode positive or electrode negative) that affects penetration, arc characteristics, and electrode performance.
example: Students selected the correct polarity for their wire type to reduce spatter and improve fusion.

definition: The conductive material that carries current to the arc; may be consumed (wire/rod) or non-consumable (tungsten).
example: Students compared a consumable wire electrode in GMAW to a tungsten electrode in GTAW.

definition: Metal added to a joint to create the weld; it becomes part of the finished weld.
example: Students confirmed the wire classification matched the base metal for the assignment.

definition: The metal being joined by welding.
example: Students cleaned mill scale from the base metal to reduce weld defects.

definition: How two parts are arranged for welding (butt, lap, tee, corner, edge) and how the joint is prepared.
example: Students chose a tee joint and added a small bevel to improve root fusion on thicker material.

definition: Preparing joint edges (cleaning, bevels, root face, root opening) to achieve proper fusion and penetration.
example: Students bevelled plate edges so the weld could penetrate to the root.

definition: The gap at the root of a joint that helps achieve full penetration when required.
example: Students set a consistent root opening using spacers before tacking.

definition: How parts are aligned and held before welding so the joint matches the intended design.
example: Students clamped and measured diagonals to keep the assembly square during tack-up.

definition: A small weld used to hold parts in position before final welding.
example: Students used four tack welds and rechecked alignment before completing full passes.

definition: One trip along the joint depositing weld metal.
example: Students used a root pass followed by fill and cap passes on a groove weld.

definition: The deposited weld metal left by a welding pass.
example: A consistent bead width showed steady travel speed and torch angle.

definition: The amount of energy delivered to the joint, influenced by current, voltage, and travel speed.
example: Students reduced heat input on thin material by increasing travel speed and adjusting settings.

definition: How fast the electrode moves along the joint; affects bead shape, penetration, and heat input.
example: Students slowed slightly to improve fusion at the toe of the fillet weld.

definition: The side-to-side angle of the electrode relative to the joint (controls bead placement and fusion).
example: Students adjusted work angle in a tee joint to keep the bead centred on both legs.

definition: The forward/back tilt of the electrode in the direction of travel (push or drag).
example: Students used a slight push angle in GMAW to improve visibility and bead profile.

definition: The length of wire extending beyond the contact tip in wire processes; affects heat and arc stability.
example: Students corrected excessive stickout to reduce spatter and improve penetration consistency.

definition: The distance between the electrode tip and the workpiece; influences heat and stability.
example: Students shortened arc length to reduce spatter and improve control on a fillet weld.

definition: How deeply the weld fuses into the base metal.
example: Students increased penetration by adjusting parameters and ensuring clean base metal.

definition: Proper melting and joining of weld metal to base metal and between passes.
example: Students corrected poor fusion by increasing heat input and reducing travel speed.

definition: The area of base metal whose properties change due to welding heat but does not melt.
example: Students used alternating weld sequence to reduce distortion and manage HAZ effects.

definition: Unwanted warping or movement caused by uneven heating and cooling.
example: Students used tack placement and alternating sides to control distortion on a frame.

definition: The orientation of the weld and workpiece (flat, horizontal, vertical, overhead).
example: Students adjusted technique and settings when moving from flat to vertical position practice.

definition: Gas used to protect the weld from atmospheric contamination in gas-shielded processes.
example: Students verified gas flow and checked for leaks before wire welding.

definition: The amount of shielding gas delivered, typically set on a flowmeter; affects porosity and coverage.
example: Students increased flow slightly after noticing porosity caused by inadequate shielding.

definition: A device that measures and sets shielding gas flow for gas-shielded welding.
example: Students set the flowmeter to the required rate before striking an arc.

definition: The area of the weld protected by shielding gas; disrupted by wind, distance, or angle.
example: Students reduced nozzle-to-work distance to improve gas coverage and reduce porosity.

definition: Gas Metal Arc Welding: a wire-feed welding process using shielding gas (often called MIG).
example: Students used GMAW for fillet weld practice on mild steel with consistent travel speed.

definition: Flux Cored Arc Welding: a wire-feed process using a flux-cored wire, sometimes with shielding gas.
example: Students used FCAW where the wire type provided slag coverage and different penetration behaviour.

definition: Shielded Metal Arc Welding: a manual arc process using a flux-coated stick electrode (often called stick welding).
example: Students practised maintaining arc length and travel speed to keep slag from trapping in the bead.

definition: Gas Tungsten Arc Welding: an arc process using a tungsten electrode and shielding gas (often called TIG).
example: Students used GTAW to practise controlled heat input and clean beads on thin material.

definition: A non-consumable electrode used in GTAW to carry current and create the arc.
example: Students prepared tungsten to the correct point so the arc stayed focused.

definition: The part in a wire welding gun that transfers current to the wire electrode.
example: Students replaced a worn contact tip when wire feeding became inconsistent.

definition: The outer piece of a wire welding gun that directs shielding gas around the arc and weld pool.
example: Students cleaned spatter from the nozzle to maintain gas coverage.

definition: The rate the wire electrode is fed; strongly affects amperage and bead shape in wire processes.
example: Students increased wire feed speed to raise amperage and improve penetration on thicker material.

definition: A parameter that affects arc length and bead profile in wire processes.
example: Students adjusted voltage to reduce spatter and improve bead wet-in at the toes.

definition: The amount of current in the welding circuit; affects heat and penetration.
example: Students selected amperage appropriate for electrode size and material thickness.

definition: How long a welder can operate at a given output within a 10-minute period before overheating.
example: Students planned weld sequence to avoid exceeding duty cycle on longer welds.

definition: The molten metal at the joint during welding that solidifies into the weld.
example: Students watched the leading edge of the weld pool to control bead size.

definition: A weld with a roughly triangular cross-section used in tee, lap, and corner joints.
example: Students measured fillet weld size to ensure it met the design requirement.

definition: A weld made in a prepared groove between two members, often used for full penetration joints.
example: Students completed a groove weld using root, fill, and cap passes.

definition: A condition that reduces weld quality or strength, often requiring correction.
example: Students identified the defect, determined the cause, and adjusted technique for the next attempt.

definition: Gas pockets in the weld caused by contamination, inadequate shielding, or incorrect parameters.
example: Students cleaned the base metal and improved gas coverage to reduce porosity.

definition: A groove melted into the base metal alongside the weld toe that is not filled with weld metal.
example: Students reduced undercut by lowering travel speed and correcting angle.

definition: Weld metal that rolls onto the base metal without fusing properly (a form of poor fusion).
example: Students corrected overlap by increasing heat input and adjusting travel angle.

definition: A failure of weld metal to properly fuse to base metal or between passes.
example: Students addressed lack of fusion by improving joint prep and increasing heat input.

definition: Insufficient depth of fusion at the root of a joint when deeper penetration is required.
example: Students adjusted root opening and technique to achieve the required penetration.

definition: Slag trapped in the weld metal, often caused by poor cleaning between passes or incorrect technique.
example: Students chipped and brushed between passes to prevent slag inclusion.

definition: Small droplets of molten metal that scatter during welding, increasing cleanup and potentially affecting quality.
example: Students reduced spatter by adjusting voltage and stickout in wire welding.

definition: A depression at the end of a weld bead that can lead to cracking if not filled properly.
example: Students paused and filled the crater before breaking the arc at the end of the weld.

definition: Removing slag, spatter, and contaminants to inspect and prepare for additional passes or finishing.
example: Students cleaned the weld and inspected for defects before adding the next pass.

definition: Cleaning between weld passes to prevent inclusions and ensure sound weld metal.
example: Students wire-brushed and chipped slag between passes on a multi-pass weld.

definition: A document that lists required variables for producing an acceptable weld (process, settings, technique, materials).
example: Students followed the WPS for wire size, gas, voltage, and travel speed range.

definition: Welding factors that must be controlled (process, polarity, parameters, joint prep, positions) to achieve quality.
example: Students recorded variables after a failed test coupon and adjusted one change at a time.

definition: Welding performed by mechanized or automated equipment for consistent, repeatable results.
example: Students identified which variables are controlled by automation versus operator setup.

definition: A welding approach where the machine feeds wire and maintains some consistency, but the operator guides the gun and controls technique.
example: Students practised steady travel speed and angles while wire feed and gas delivery were machine-controlled.

definition: Welding on round or tubular components where fit-up, position, and joint consistency are critical.
example: Students maintained consistent root opening and controlled heat input to avoid burn-through on pipe.

definition: Thin metal stock supplied in flat sheets, commonly used for enclosures, panels, and ducting.
example: Students selected sheet thickness that could be formed on available shop equipment without cracking.

definition: A common sheet metal thickness system where a higher gauge number typically means thinner material (varies by metal type).
example: Students confirmed both gauge and actual thickness before setting the shear and brake.

definition: The measured distance between the two faces of sheet metal, used to set tooling and determine bend allowances.
example: Students measured thickness to choose the correct die opening for bending.

definition: The direction of metal’s rolling pattern, which affects how a sheet bends and resists cracking.
example: Students oriented the part so critical bends were made with the grain when possible.

definition: Marking a flat pattern on sheet metal to guide cutting, punching, and forming.
example: Students laid out bend lines and hole centres before cutting the blank.

definition: A piece of sheet metal cut to size before forming operations begin.
example: Students cut a blank slightly oversized, then trimmed to final size after forming.

definition: A 2D layout of a part before it is bent or formed, including allowances for bends and seams.
example: Students created a flat pattern for a tray so the final dimensions matched after bending.

definition: A marked line showing where a sheet will be bent during forming.
example: Students aligned the bend line to the brake’s reference edge before bending.

definition: Extra material length added in a flat pattern to account for stretching in the bend region.
example: Students calculated bend allowance so the finished box sides were the correct length.

definition: The amount subtracted from outside dimensions in a flat pattern to account for material taken up in the bend.
example: Students used bend deduction to convert finished outside dimensions into correct blank size.

definition: A value used in bend calculations that describes where the neutral axis sits within the thickness during bending.
example: Students used a typical K-factor for mild steel to estimate bend allowance for a project part.

definition: The layer within the sheet thickness that does not stretch or compress during bending.
example: Students discussed how the neutral axis shifts based on material and tooling.

definition: The radius formed on the inside of a bend; influenced by tooling and material thickness.
example: Students selected tooling that produced an inside bend radius appropriate for the material to avoid cracking.

definition: The tendency of sheet metal to slightly unbend after forming due to elasticity.
example: Students overbent slightly to compensate for springback and hit the target angle.

definition: The final angle formed in the sheet after bending.
example: Students checked bend angle with an angle gauge and adjusted setup for consistency.

definition: A machine that bends sheet metal using a punch and die set.
example: Students set the back gauge and aligned bend lines to produce repeatable bends.

definition: The upper tooling on a brake that presses into the material to form a bend.
example: Students selected a punch profile that matched the desired inside radius.

definition: The lower tooling on a brake that supports the material and forms the bend shape.
example: Students chose die opening based on thickness to reduce cracking and improve accuracy.

definition: The width of the die opening used in bending; affects bend radius, tonnage, and accuracy.
example: Students used a wider die opening for thicker sheet to reduce required force.

definition: A bending method where the sheet contacts the punch tip and die shoulders but does not bottom out in the die.
example: Students used air bending to achieve multiple angles using the same punch and die set.

definition: A bending method where the sheet is pressed deeper into the die to form a more fixed angle than air bending.
example: Students used bottoming to improve repeatability for identical parts.

definition: A high-force bending method that permanently sets the bend by compressing material in the bend region.
example: Students discussed coining as a method that reduces springback but requires higher tonnage.

definition: An adjustable stop on a brake used to position the sheet for consistent bend locations.
example: Students set the back gauge so all flanges were the same depth across a batch.

definition: The force required to make a bend, influenced by thickness, material type, die opening, and bend length.
example: Students checked tonnage limits to ensure the brake could safely form the part.

definition: Cutting sheet metal with a straight blade action, producing a clean, fast cut.
example: Students used the shear to cut blanks to size before forming.

definition: A shear setup that uses a squaring arm/guide to produce accurate 90-degree cuts.
example: Students used the squaring arm to keep blanks square for box and tray projects.

definition: Removing a section of material, often at corners, to allow folding and assembly.
example: Students notched corners so flanges could fold without interference.

definition: A notch or cut-out at a corner that reduces tearing and distortion during bending.
example: Students added corner relief to prevent bulging at flange intersections.

definition: A sharp raised edge left after cutting or punching that must be removed for safety and fit.
example: Students deburred edges after shearing to prevent cuts and improve assembly.

definition: Smoothing or conditioning edges after cutting to meet safety and quality requirements.
example: Students used a file and abrasive pad to break sharp edges on a panel.

definition: Creating openings in sheet metal by drilling, punching, or cutting processes.
example: Students chose punching for speed on repeated holes, and drilling for small batches.

definition: Creating holes by shearing material with a punch and die set, often faster than drilling for production work.
example: Students used a punch to make clean holes for rivets in sheet assemblies.

definition: Making holes using a drill bit; requires support to prevent grabbing and distortion.
example: Students backed sheet metal with scrap to reduce burrs and prevent the bit from grabbing.

definition: A drill bit with stepped diameters used to create clean holes in thin material.
example: Students used a step drill to enlarge holes without tearing the sheet.

definition: A conical recess that allows a flat-head fastener to sit flush with the surface.
example: Students countersunk holes for flush fasteners on a panel surface.

definition: A flat-bottom recess that allows a fastener head to sit below or flush with the surface.
example: Students counterbored holes to recess bolt heads where clearance was required.

definition: Joining sheet parts using fasteners rather than welding, often for serviceability and distortion control.
example: Students used rivets for a thin enclosure to reduce heat distortion.

definition: A permanent mechanical fastener used to join sheet materials by deforming a shank to clamp parts together.
example: Students selected rivet length so it formed correctly without crushing the sheet.

definition: A rivet installed from one side of the workpiece (commonly called a pop rivet).
example: Students used blind rivets when the inside of the enclosure was not accessible.

definition: The distance between rivets, affecting joint strength and distortion control.
example: Students followed a consistent rivet spacing pattern along a seam for uniform strength.

definition: A joint in sheet metal where edges meet or overlap, often folded or fastened.
example: Students created a seam to join two sheet edges before fastening and finishing.

definition: A folded edge that reinforces a panel and removes sharp edges.
example: Students hemmed the panel edge so it was safer to handle and more rigid.

definition: A bent edge that adds stiffness, provides attachment surfaces, or forms an enclosure.
example: Students added flanges to a tray to improve rigidity and provide mounting points.

definition: A stepped form used to align surfaces or create clearance between sheet sections.
example: Students formed an offset so overlapping panels sat flush in an assembly.

definition: A formed ridge that increases stiffness without adding thickness.
example: Students added a bead to a large panel to reduce oil-canning and vibration.

definition: Planning and creating accurate flat patterns for formed shapes, including allowances and relief cuts.
example: Students developed patterns for a box and verified dimensions before production cutting.

definition: The ability to produce the same part consistently across multiple units.
example: Students used back gauge settings and a bend sequence to make repeated parts match.

definition: The planned order of bends to avoid interference with tooling and to maintain accuracy.
example: Students bent small flanges first so the part still fit the brake for later bends.

definition: When a partially formed part contacts tooling or machine components and prevents correct forming.
example: Students changed bend sequence to avoid the flange hitting the punch during a later bend.

definition: An issue created during forming such as cracking, tearing, excessive springback, or distorted geometry.
example: Edge cracking led students to increase bend radius and check grain direction.

definition: A process area where metal is melted and poured into moulds to create cast parts.
example: Students planned the foundry workflow: pattern prep, mould making, melt, pour, cool, and finishing.

definition: Making a part by pouring molten metal into a mould and allowing it to solidify.
example: Students cast a simple part, then removed gates and cleaned the casting for inspection.

definition: A model of the part used to create the mould cavity; typically slightly oversized to account for shrinkage and machining.
example: Students used a pattern to form a sand mould cavity for a class casting project.

definition: Intentional size and shape adjustments built into a pattern (shrinkage, draft, machining allowance, distortion).
example: Students added machining allowance so the final surface could be filed or machined to size after casting.

definition: Extra size added to a pattern to account for metal contraction as it cools and solidifies.
example: Students selected a shrinkage allowance based on the metal being cast.

definition: Extra material added to cast surfaces that will be finished by machining or filing after casting.
example: Students left extra stock on a surface so it could be flattened after casting.

definition: A slight taper on vertical surfaces of a pattern to help it release from the mould without tearing sand.
example: Students added draft to the pattern so it could be removed cleanly from the mould.

definition: The line where mould halves meet and separate (cope and drag).
example: Students planned the parting line to reduce undercuts and improve mould removal.

definition: The top half of a two-part sand mould.
example: Students placed the cope on the drag and aligned the mould halves before pouring.

definition: The bottom half of a two-part sand mould.
example: Students packed sand into the drag and levelled the surface before setting the cope.

definition: A rigid frame that holds the sand mould (cope and drag sections).
example: Students clamped the flask securely so the mould stayed aligned during the pour.

definition: The hollow space in the mould that forms the shape of the casting.
example: Students inspected the mould cavity for broken edges before assembling the mould.

definition: A shaped insert placed in the mould to form internal cavities or holes in the casting.
example: Students used a core to create a hollow section that could not be formed by the pattern alone.

definition: A feature on a pattern that supports and locates a core in the correct position.
example: Students relied on core prints so the core did not shift during assembly or pour.

definition: Moist moulding sand (sand, clay binder, water) used to form moulds that hold shape when packed.
example: Students checked green sand moisture so it packed well and held detail without crumbling.

definition: A material added to sand to help it hold together and keep mould shape.
example: Students adjusted binder content so the mould maintained edges during pattern removal.

definition: Packing sand around a pattern to create a strong mould with good detail.
example: Students rammed evenly to avoid soft spots that could wash out during pouring.

definition: Small passages that allow gases and steam to escape from the mould during pouring.
example: Students vented the cope to reduce gas defects in the casting.

definition: The main vertical channel that molten metal flows through into the mould.
example: Students cut a sprue that fed smoothly without breaking mould walls.

definition: A horizontal channel that carries molten metal from the sprue to the gate(s).
example: Students designed runners to deliver metal to the cavity without excessive turbulence.

definition: The entry point where molten metal flows from the runner into the mould cavity.
example: Students positioned the gate to reduce erosion and help fill the cavity evenly.

definition: A reservoir of molten metal that feeds the casting as it shrinks during solidification, reducing shrinkage voids.
example: Students placed a riser near the thickest section to feed it during cooling.

definition: A material placed in a mould to increase cooling rate in a specific area and control solidification.
example: Students used a chill to help a thicker section solidify more evenly and reduce defects.

definition: Chaotic metal flow that can trap gas and erode mould surfaces, increasing defects.
example: Students poured steadily to reduce turbulence and avoid sand inclusions.

definition: A reservoir at the top of the sprue that helps control flow and reduce aspiration/turbulence.
example: Students used a pouring basin to maintain a stable metal head during the pour.

definition: A tool used to transport and pour molten metal safely.
example: Students preheated the ladle and used a controlled pour into the sprue.

definition: A heat-resistant container used to melt metal in a furnace.
example: Students inspected the crucible for cracks before charging it with metal.

definition: Equipment used to heat and melt metal to a pouring temperature.
example: Students followed the furnace start-up procedure and monitored melt progress.

definition: The metal placed into a crucible or furnace to be melted.
example: Students prepared a clean charge by removing contaminants and sorting by metal type.

definition: The temperature range at which metal is poured to fill the mould properly without excessive defects.
example: Students aimed for proper pouring temperature so the metal filled detail without cold shuts.

definition: The change from liquid metal to solid metal during cooling in the mould.
example: Students discussed why thick sections solidify slower and need feeding from a riser.

definition: How quickly the casting cools, affecting grain structure, strength, and defect formation.
example: Students compared cooling rate effects between thin and thick casting sections.

definition: A defect where two metal fronts meet but do not fuse, often due to low temperature or poor gating.
example: Students identified a cold shut line and suggested increasing pouring temperature or improving gating.

definition: A casting defect where the mould is not completely filled.
example: A misrun led students to adjust pouring technique and check venting and temperature.

definition: A void caused by metal contraction during solidification when there is insufficient feeding.
example: Students traced a shrinkage cavity to poor riser placement near a thick section.

definition: Small holes in a casting caused by trapped gases from moisture, turbulence, or contamination.
example: Students reduced gas porosity by improving venting and avoiding overly wet sand.

definition: Sand trapped in the casting due to mould erosion, poor ramming, or turbulent flow.
example: Students improved ramming and reduced turbulence to prevent sand inclusions.

definition: A crack that forms during solidification when metal cannot contract freely.
example: Students identified a hot tear and discussed improving mould design to allow contraction.

definition: A defect where sand fuses to the casting surface due to high temperature or sand issues.
example: Students removed burn-on during finishing and reviewed sand condition to prevent recurrence.

definition: Removing the casting from the mould after it has cooled sufficiently.
example: Students waited for safe temperature, then performed shakeout and collected sand for reuse or disposal.

definition: Cutting or breaking off gates and runners from a casting after shakeout.
example: Students removed gates and runners, then ground the stubs flush as required.

definition: Cleaning and finishing a casting by removing excess material and improving surface quality.
example: Students fettled the casting by grinding flash and smoothing rough areas before inspection.

definition: Thin excess metal that leaks into mould parting lines or gaps.
example: Students removed flash at the parting line during finishing operations.

definition: Checking key measurements of a casting against intended dimensions after cooling and finishing.
example: Students measured critical features to decide whether additional finishing or machining was required.

definition: Specialized protection for molten metal work (face shield, heat-resistant gloves, leathers, footwear, eye protection).
example: Students wore foundry PPE during pouring and maintained safe spacing around the pour area.

definition: The risk of violent steam expansion and spatter if molten metal contacts moisture.
example: Students ensured tools and scrap were dry before charging and pouring to prevent eruptions.

definition: Removing material in a controlled way to produce accurate sizes, shapes, and surface finishes.
example: Students machined a part to final dimension by facing, drilling, and turning to meet tolerance.

definition: How quickly material is removed during machining, affected by speed, feed, depth of cut, and tooling.
example: Students reduced depth of cut to lower the material removal rate and improve surface finish.

definition: Securing the workpiece so it can be machined safely and accurately.
example: Students checked that stock was seated and clamped before turning to avoid the part shifting.

definition: A reference surface, point, or axis used to locate and measure features during machining.
example: Students established a datum face by facing the part before measuring length features.

definition: The allowable variation from a target dimension.
example: Students machined to a tolerance by taking a finishing pass and measuring frequently.

definition: The texture and smoothness of a machined surface, influenced by tool condition and machining parameters.
example: Students improved surface finish by reducing feed rate and using a sharp tool.

definition: A sharp raised edge left after cutting or machining operations.
example: Students removed burrs from a drilled hole so a shaft would fit smoothly.

definition: A piece of material removed during machining.
example: Students used a brush to clear chips rather than hands to prevent cuts.

definition: Managing chip size and shape to improve safety, finish, and tool life.
example: Students adjusted feed and depth of cut to prevent long stringy chips from wrapping the tool.

definition: Fluid used to cool, lubricate, and help remove chips during machining.
example: Students applied cutting fluid while drilling to reduce heat and improve tool life.

definition: Spindle rotation rate, measured in revolutions per minute, affecting cutting action and heat.
example: Students lowered RPM when machining larger diameters to maintain safe cutting conditions.

definition: The speed of the cutting edge relative to the workpiece surface, based on RPM and diameter.
example: Students increased surface speed for aluminum compared to steel to improve finish.

definition: How fast the tool advances into or across the workpiece, affecting finish and chip load.
example: Students reduced feed rate for a finishing pass to achieve a smoother surface.

definition: How much material the tool removes in one pass, affecting load and tool wear.
example: Students used a shallow depth of cut for finishing to maintain tolerance.

definition: A machine that rotates the workpiece while a cutting tool removes material to create cylindrical shapes.
example: Students used the lathe to face the end of stock and turn to diameter.

definition: A machine that rotates a cutting tool to remove material from a stationary workpiece, creating flats, slots, and profiles.
example: Students used the milling machine to cut a keyway slot to a specified width.

definition: The rotating component of a machine tool that holds and drives a chuck, collet, or toolholder.
example: Students verified spindle direction and speed before engaging the cut.

definition: A clamping device on a lathe spindle used to hold the workpiece (often a three-jaw or four-jaw).
example: Students ensured the chuck key was removed immediately after tightening.

definition: A key used to tighten or loosen a chuck; must never be left in the chuck.
example: Students performed a visual check to confirm the chuck key was removed before starting the lathe.

definition: A precision clamping device used to hold round stock or tooling with strong concentricity.
example: Students used a collet to hold small-diameter stock with minimal runout.

definition: A device that holds and positions a cutting tool securely.
example: Students checked toolholder tightness to prevent chatter during a turning pass.

definition: The angles and shape of a cutting tool that affect chip formation, cutting forces, and finish.
example: Students selected a tool with appropriate rake for aluminum to reduce built-up edge.

definition: Gradual loss of cutting edge quality that reduces finish and accuracy.
example: Students replaced a dull tool after noticing increased cutting force and poor finish.

definition: Vibration during cutting that leaves a rough finish and can damage tools or work.
example: Students reduced chatter by tightening workholding and adjusting speed and depth of cut.

definition: Machining the end of a workpiece flat and square to its axis on a lathe.
example: Students faced the stock to create a clean datum surface before turning to length.

definition: Reducing the diameter of a rotating workpiece on a lathe using a cutting tool.
example: Students turned the shaft to final diameter and verified size with a micrometer.

definition: Creating a conical surface on a lathe by changing the tool path relative to the work axis.
example: Students produced a taper to match a mating component requirement.

definition: Cutting a finished part off from stock on a lathe using a parting tool.
example: Students used cutting fluid and steady feed to part off without binding.

definition: Rolling a patterned texture onto a cylindrical surface to improve grip.
example: Students knurled a handle section to make it easier to hold with gloves.

definition: Enlarging and finishing an existing hole on a lathe to improve accuracy and surface finish.
example: Students bored a hole to a precise diameter for a press fit.

definition: Finishing a drilled hole to an accurate diameter and improved finish using a reamer.
example: Students reamed a hole so a pin fit smoothly without wobble.

definition: Creating a hole using a drill bit, often as a first step before reaming or tapping.
example: Students centre-drilled, then drilled to depth before reaming to final size.

definition: Using a short, rigid centre drill to start an accurate hole and create a lead-in for drilling.
example: Students centre-drilled to prevent the main drill bit from wandering.

definition: Cutting internal threads in a hole using a tap.
example: Students tapped a drilled hole to create threads for a bolt connection.

definition: The distance between threads (or threads per inch) that must match the fastener.
example: Students checked thread pitch before tapping to ensure the correct bolt would fit.

definition: Removing material with a rotating multi-edge cutter to create flats, slots, and contours.
example: Students milled a flat surface to create a datum before cutting a slot feature.

definition: A milling cutter used for slotting, profiling, and facing operations.
example: Students selected a two-flute end mill for aluminum to improve chip clearing.

definition: A cutter used to machine large flat surfaces efficiently.
example: Students used a face mill to flatten a plate to consistent thickness.

definition: A narrow opening machined into a part, often for keys, tabs, or clearance.
example: Students milled a slot to fit a matching tab with minimal play.

definition: A specific slot that accepts a key to prevent relative rotation between a shaft and hub.
example: Students machined a keyway to match the specified key size for torque transfer.

definition: Tools used to verify dimensions and tolerance (calipers, micrometers, indicators).
example: Students measured diameter with a micrometer for higher precision than calipers.

definition: A measuring tool used for outside, inside, and depth measurements.
example: Students used calipers to check rough dimensions before a finishing pass.

definition: A precision measuring tool used for very accurate outside (and other) measurements.
example: Students used a micrometer to verify final shaft diameter within tight tolerance.

definition: A precision instrument used to measure small movements and check runout, alignment, or flatness.
example: Students used a dial indicator to check runout before finishing a turning operation.

definition: Wobble or deviation from true rotation, causing accuracy and finish issues.
example: Students corrected runout by reseating the stock and checking chuck clamping.

definition: Computer Numerical Control: machines that follow programmed instructions to cut parts accurately and repeatably.
example: Students used CNC to produce multiple identical parts with consistent dimensions.

definition: The common programming language used to control CNC machine motions and functions.
example: Students reviewed G-code commands to confirm safe tool paths before running the program.

definition: A defined coordinate reference used by CNC to locate the part relative to the machine.
example: Students set the WCS so the program’s origin matched the part datum corner.

definition: The machine’s fixed reference point used to establish coordinates and travel limits.
example: Students referenced machine zero when setting up offsets and verifying travel range.

definition: The chosen origin point for a CNC job, set on the workpiece or fixture.
example: Students set work zero at the top corner of stock to simplify toolpath programming.

definition: A stored value that accounts for tool length/diameter so CNC can cut accurately.
example: Students measured a tool and entered offsets before running the first operation.

definition: The programmed route a cutting tool follows to remove material.
example: Students simulated the toolpath to ensure it cleared clamps and avoided collisions.

definition: Running a CNC program without cutting (or at safe height) to check movement and safety.
example: Students performed a dry run to confirm the toolpath cleared the vise and fixtures.

definition: Unwanted contact between tool, workpiece, fixture, or machine components during CNC operation.
example: Students prevented collision by verifying offsets and running a simulation first.

definition: Programmed feed rate and spindle speed values that affect tool load, finish, and safety.
example: Students reduced feed rate on a finishing toolpath to improve surface finish.

definition: Shaping metal by applying force (hammering or pressing), usually while the metal is hot, to change its form and structure.
example: Students forged a tapered section by heating steel and drawing it out on the anvil.

definition: Deforming metal at elevated temperature so it is easier to shape and less likely to crack.
example: Students reheated the workpiece to maintain hot-working temperature before continuing shaping.

definition: A heating unit used to bring metal to a workable temperature for forging.
example: Students used the forge to heat the steel evenly before starting hammer work.

definition: A heavy steel work surface used for shaping and supporting hot metal during forging.
example: Students used the anvil face for flattening and the horn for forming curves.

definition: A tool used to deliver controlled blows to shape hot metal.
example: Students used consistent hammer strikes to keep the taper even and centred.

definition: Gripping tools used to hold and control hot metal safely.
example: Students used tongs to keep hands away from heat while rotating the workpiece.

definition: Rapid cooling of hot metal in a medium (water, oil, etc.) to change properties or stop heat effects.
example: Students quenched between heats to stop scaling on a surface they needed to preserve.

definition: Oxide buildup on hot steel surfaces caused by exposure to air at high temperature.
example: Students wire-brushed scale between heats to keep surfaces clean and reduce defects.

definition: A visual indicator of temperature on hot metal (used as a practical guide for working range).
example: Students used heat colour to decide when to reheat rather than hammering too cold.

definition: The temperature span where a metal can be forged effectively without cracking or burning.
example: Students avoided striking the steel below its working range to prevent cracking.

definition: Heating metal too hot, damaging structure and increasing the risk of cracking or failure.
example: Students reduced forge time and controlled airflow to avoid burning the steel edges.

definition: A forging operation that lengthens metal while reducing its cross-section.
example: Students drew out a bar to make a longer, thinner section for a hook.

definition: A forging operation that shortens metal while increasing its cross-section (thickening).
example: Students upset the end of a bar to create more mass for a head or shoulder.

definition: Forming a curve or angle in hot metal using controlled force and support surfaces.
example: Students bent the workpiece over the anvil horn to form a smooth curve.

definition: Rotating a heated section to create a spiral form while keeping the rest of the part aligned.
example: Students twisted the bar evenly using a twisting wrench and consistent heat.

definition: Using a fuller tool or edge to create grooves and move material efficiently during forging.
example: Students used fullering to define a transition before drawing out a taper.

definition: Smoothing and thinning a section using controlled hammer blows on the anvil face.
example: Students flattened a section to a target thickness before final shaping.

definition: Creating a hole in hot metal using a punch tool, often followed by drifting to size.
example: Students punched a hole, then drifted it to final size for a rivet or handle fit.

definition: Enlarging and shaping a punched hole using a drift tool to reach final size and shape.
example: Students used a drift to make the hole round and consistent before cooling.

definition: An anvil-mounted tool inserted into the hardy hole for cutting, bending, or shaping operations.
example: Students used a hardy cut-off tool to hot-cut stock to length.

definition: Cutting metal while it is hot using chisels or anvil tools.
example: Students hot-cut the end of a bar, then returned it to the forge to reheat.

definition: Heating and air-cooling steel to refine grain structure and relieve stresses after forging.
example: Students normalized a forged piece to reduce internal stress before final finishing.

definition: The direction of the metal’s internal structure, often improved by forging for strength along the part shape.
example: Students discussed how forging can align grain flow with the part’s shape for durability.

definition: Reducing internal stresses created by heating and deformation to prevent warping or cracking later.
example: After forging, students used a controlled cool-down to reduce stress and distortion.

definition: Protective gear for hot work (eye protection, heat-resistant gloves, leathers, proper footwear, hearing protection).
example: Students wore forging PPE to protect against scale, sparks, and hot material contact.

definition: Practices for safely moving, placing, and setting down hot metal to prevent burns and fires.
example: Students placed hot steel only on designated surfaces and communicated ‘hot’ clearly to others.

definition: Building one-off or small-run parts to meet specific requirements, often requiring planning, fit-up, and problem-solving.
example: Students produced a custom bracket by measuring the mounting location, drafting a plan, and fabricating to fit.

definition: Producing components in advance (often in a shop) so they can be assembled efficiently on site or later in a build.
example: Students prefabricated identical frame sections to reduce on-site assembly time and improve consistency.

definition: Planning, measuring, cutting, assembling, and installing piping systems using fittings and alignment methods.
example: Students built a simple piping layout and verified alignment before final tightening and support placement.

definition: A clear description of what the job includes, what it excludes, and what ‘done’ looks like.
example: Students wrote a scope of work that specified dimensions, mounting points, finish level, and timeline.

definition: Detailed requirements a product or installation must meet (dimensions, materials, tolerances, standards).
example: Students checked specifications before cutting stock to ensure correct material size and finish requirements.

definition: Measuring real-world conditions to confirm fit before fabrication or installation.
example: Students measured a mounting location and confirmed clearance before building the component.

definition: The actual real-world state of a site or assembly, which may differ from plans or ideal dimensions.
example: Students adjusted their part because as-built conditions showed the mounting surface was not square.

definition: The combined effect of small measurement and fabrication variations across multiple parts or steps.
example: Students used baseline measurements and jigs to reduce tolerance stack-up across repeated parts.

definition: A working drawing used to build a part, including dimensions, materials, and assembly details.
example: Students created a fabrication drawing to communicate cut lengths and hole locations to another group.

definition: A list of components to cut, including lengths, quantities, and identification labels for assembly or install.
example: Students produced a cut list and labelled each part so the install sequence was clear.

definition: Estimating and listing materials and quantities needed based on drawings or measurements.
example: Students completed a material takeoff for pipe, fittings, fasteners, and supports before starting work.

definition: Labelling parts so they can be tracked, assembled correctly, and matched to documentation.
example: Students marked each piece with an ID that matched the cut list and assembly plan.

definition: Aligning and holding parts so they match the intended design before fastening or welding.
example: Students used clamps and squares to fit up a frame so diagonals matched before final assembly.

definition: Planning how parts will be held and referenced to maintain alignment and repeatability.
example: Students built a simple fixture so multiple assemblies stayed square during fabrication.

definition: The planned order of steps used to build or install components to avoid interference and reduce rework.
example: Students assembled sub-components first, then installed the full unit to reduce awkward fastening.

definition: A conflict where parts collide or cannot be installed due to clearance or geometry issues.
example: Students changed the order of installation when a support bracket blocked access to a fastener.

definition: Positioning parts so they are straight, square, and correctly oriented to their reference points.
example: Students used a level and square to align the assembly before final tightening.

definition: A condition where a surface is horizontal relative to gravity, commonly checked during installation.
example: Students checked a support rail with a level before fastening it permanently.

definition: A condition where a surface is vertical relative to gravity.
example: Students verified the post was plumb before tightening anchors and braces.

definition: A condition where two lines or surfaces meet at 90 degrees; critical for frames and layouts.
example: Students measured diagonals to confirm a rectangular assembly was square before securing it.

definition: A component that holds, braces, or carries load for an assembly or piping system.
example: Students installed supports to prevent pipe sag and reduce stress on fittings.

definition: A fastener or device used to secure an assembly to a structure such as concrete or wood.
example: Students selected anchors appropriate for the mounting surface and required load.

definition: Planning clear space so tools can reach fasteners for assembly, inspection, and maintenance.
example: Students positioned a bracket so fasteners could be tightened and later serviced without disassembly.

definition: A standard that indicates pipe wall thickness for a given nominal size (affects strength and weight).
example: Students verified pipe schedule so fittings and supports matched the required rating.

definition: A standardized pipe size naming system that does not equal the exact measured outside diameter.
example: Students used NPS to select matching fittings rather than relying on measured diameter alone.

definition: A component used to connect, change direction, branch, or transition pipe size/type.
example: Students used elbows and tees to build a layout that met the required route.

definition: A pipe fitting that changes direction, commonly 45° or 90°.
example: Students used a 90° elbow to route pipe around an obstruction while maintaining clearance.

definition: A fitting that creates a branch connection from a main pipe run.
example: Students installed a tee to add a branch line while keeping the main line aligned.

definition: A fitting used to connect two different pipe sizes.
example: Students installed a reducer to transition from the main line to a smaller branch line.

definition: Planning a piping route and components to meet function, clearance, and support requirements.
example: Students planned pipe layout to avoid interference with other components and allow maintenance access.

definition: The amount of length consumed by fittings and threads/weld prep that must be accounted for in cut lengths.
example: Students adjusted cut lengths to account for take-up so final overall length matched the drawing.

definition: Cutting components based on real measurements and fitting conditions rather than relying only on nominal lengths.
example: Students cut-to-fit the final section after confirming the actual installed distance on site.

definition: Verifying dimensions, alignment, support, and workmanship before sign-off or use.
example: Students performed a quality check: level, plumb, alignment, fastener tightness, and safe edges.

definition: Correcting work that does not meet requirements, often due to measurement, fit-up, or sequence errors.
example: A misaligned bracket required rework: loosening, repositioning, and re-fastening to specification.

definition: A final verification that an installed assembly functions as intended and is safe for use.
example: Students confirmed the assembly operated smoothly, was secure, and met clearance requirements.

definition: A controlled area for installation or assembly that reduces risk to people and prevents damage.
example: Students set a safe work zone with clear walkways and marked hazards during installation work.

definition: Building one-off or small-run parts to meet specific requirements, often requiring planning, fit-up, and problem-solving.
example: Students produced a custom bracket by measuring the mounting location, drafting a plan, and fabricating to fit.

definition: Producing components in advance (often in a shop) so they can be assembled efficiently on site or later in a build.
example: Students prefabricated identical frame sections to reduce on-site assembly time and improve consistency.

definition: Planning, measuring, cutting, assembling, and installing piping systems using fittings and alignment methods.
example: Students built a simple piping layout and verified alignment before final tightening and support placement.

definition: A clear description of what the job includes, what it excludes, and what ‘done’ looks like.
example: Students wrote a scope of work that specified dimensions, mounting points, finish level, and timeline.

definition: Detailed requirements a product or installation must meet (dimensions, materials, tolerances, standards).
example: Students checked specifications before cutting stock to ensure correct material size and finish requirements.

definition: Measuring real-world conditions to confirm fit before fabrication or installation.
example: Students measured a mounting location and confirmed clearance before building the component.

definition: The actual real-world state of a site or assembly, which may differ from plans or ideal dimensions.
example: Students adjusted their part because as-built conditions showed the mounting surface was not square.

definition: The combined effect of small measurement and fabrication variations across multiple parts or steps.
example: Students used baseline measurements and jigs to reduce tolerance stack-up across repeated parts.

definition: A working drawing used to build a part, including dimensions, materials, and assembly details.
example: Students created a fabrication drawing to communicate cut lengths and hole locations to another group.

definition: A list of components to cut, including lengths, quantities, and identification labels for assembly or install.
example: Students produced a cut list and labelled each part so the install sequence was clear.

definition: Estimating and listing materials and quantities needed based on drawings or measurements.
example: Students completed a material takeoff for pipe, fittings, fasteners, and supports before starting work.

definition: Labelling parts so they can be tracked, assembled correctly, and matched to documentation.
example: Students marked each piece with an ID that matched the cut list and assembly plan.

definition: Aligning and holding parts so they match the intended design before fastening or welding.
example: Students used clamps and squares to fit up a frame so diagonals matched before final assembly.

definition: Planning how parts will be held and referenced to maintain alignment and repeatability.
example: Students built a simple fixture so multiple assemblies stayed square during fabrication.
